nodes.label: Philip C. C. Huang
nodes.date_label: Modern China founded 1975 · The Peasant Economy and Social Change in North China 1985 · The Peasant Family and Rural Development in the Yangzi Delta 1990 · “The Paradigmatic Crisis in Chinese Studies” 1991 · Civil Justice in China 1996 · Code, Custom, and Legal Practice 2001 · exchange with Pomeranz 2002–2003
nodes.description: A historian of rural China and Chinese law and the founding editor of Modern China (1975). Huang argued that Ming–Qing commercialization proceeded without capitalist development through involution: output per unit of land rose while the marginal returns to additional labour on family farms diminished, “growth without development”, a claim about marginal rather than average productivity that his critics contested. He took the term from Clifford Geertz’s “agricultural involution” and the mechanism partly from Chayanov, as he acknowledged in 1985 and again in 1991. The Peasant Economy and Social Change in North China (1985) and The Peasant Family and Rural Development in the Yangzi Delta (1990) developed the argument, and “The Paradigmatic Crisis in Chinese Studies” (1991) held that Western and Chinese models, Marxist “incipient capitalism” among them, shared assumptions that Chinese evidence made “paradoxical”. His legal histories include Civil Justice in China (1996) and Code, Custom, and Legal Practice in China (2001). He took “practice” from Bourdieu while preferring “the study of practice as historical process” (2005), and rejected culturalist claims, which he attributed to Said, that facts are “no more than representations” (1998). After 2000 he was a prominent critic of Kenneth Pomeranz, arguing that eighteenth-century England and the Yangzi delta stood “at opposite poles in a continuum from development to involution” (2002); Pomeranz answered that involution was “internally inconsistent” (2003).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Philip C. C. Huang; The Peasant Economy and Social Change in North China (1985); The Peasant Family and Rural Development in the Yangzi Delta, 1350–1988 (1990); “The Paradigmatic Crisis in Chinese Studies: Paradoxes in Social and Economic History” (Modern China, 1991); Civil Justice in China (1996); Code, Custom, and Legal Practice in China (2001); “Development or Involution in Eighteenth-Century Britain and China?” (Journal of Asian Studies, 2002) and “Further Thoughts on Eighteenth-Century Britain and China” (2003); “Theory and the Study of Modern Chinese History: Four Traps and a Question” (1998); “Divorce Law Practices and the Origins, Myths, and Realities of Judicial ‘Mediation’ in China” (2005); “Our Sense of Problem” (2016). Founding editor of Modern China (1975). Readings: Mann’s and Duara’s reviews (1986); Pomeranz’s replies (2002, 2003).
nodes.scope_note: Involution is presented as Huang defined it in the 1985 book (pp. 7–11 read) and restated it in 1991 (pp. 299–302 and 314–317 read), 2002 (whole article OCRed; selected passages read closely, remaining text searched; map images not inspected) and 2003 (pp. 157–158 and 164–165 read). The 1990 book is unread; it is known through those restatements, Pomeranz’s citation of its pp. 11–17 and Day’s review. Geertz and Chayanov are his acknowledged resources (1985, p. 8; 1991, p. 317) and Boserup a third (1991, n. 9); he redefined Geertz’s term. The exchange with Pomeranz appears once, as two critique arrows. Huang conceded a misplaced decimal in the 1990 book (2003, p. 157) and, as he reports it, Pomeranz’s reply granted declining average returns as cotton displaced grain. Brenner and Isett (2002) and the real-wage study of Allen and colleagues (2011) side partly with him on living standards and divergence, not on the mechanism. His legal histories of 1996 and 2001 are dated only and their arguments are unread here; his use of Bourdieu’s “practice” is taken from a 2005 note and a 1995 article read in part by a second research pass, and his wider later work on practice falls outside this reading. His 1998 critique of Said is read at pp. 193–195. Life dates are not established from texts read.

edges.relationship: Geertz’s “agricultural involution” (Java, 1963), with Chayanov’s account of family-labour intensification, taken as the model for involution in North China (1985) and the Yangzi delta, as Huang acknowledged (1985, 1991)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, in period. The Peasant Economy and Social Change in North China (1985, pp. 7–11 read): "Chayanov pointed out the existence of this phenomenon in the agriculture of prerevolutionary Russia … Clifford Geertz has given the same phenomenon, in rice farming in Java, the catchy term 'agricultural involution' (1963)" (p. 8); "The peasant economy, in other words, involuted along the lines suggested by Geertz's analytical model" (p. 11). "The Paradigmatic Crisis in Chinese Studies" (1991, p. 317): "my notion of involution has drawn much from the theories of A. V. Chayanov and Clifford Geertz, both based on micro-social studies of non-Western societies." Readers in 1986 confirm it: Mann, "a model of agricultural involution derived partly from Geertz and partly from Chayanov" (JAS, p. 572); Duara, "Huang uses Clifford Geertz's notion of involution" (HJAS, p. 285). Qualifications: Chayanov (no entry) is an equal resource and Boserup a third (1991, n. 9); Huang redefines the term as diminishing marginal returns to labour on family farms (1985, p. 8 n.) and does not adopt Geertz's ecological argument about Java. This is Geertz's Agricultural Involution, not the interpretive anthropology of thick description recorded on the geertz entry.
edges.map_label: Agricultural involution, Java to North China, 1985

edges.relationship: Involution and involutionary commercialization: output growth at diminishing returns per workday on family farms, “growth without development” (1985, 1990, 1991)
edges.evidence_note: His own statements, read. 1985 (pp. 8–9): involution occurs when "the marginal output of labor diminishes", and is rational as "both enterprise behavior and consumer choice"; peasant behaviour needs "the integrated use of the formalist, Marxist, and substantivist traditions". 1991 (pp. 314–315): "Shrinking farm sizes drove peasants to accept involution, or intensification of labor input per unit area at the cost of diminishing marginal returns per workday"; "Involution, in other words, explains the paradox of growth without development"; involutionary commercialization "needs to be distinguished from the transformative commercialization that ends in modern development". 2002 (p. 503) restates the 1990 book's distinction between development, involution and intensification ("(1990, 11)"). The 1990 book is unread: Day's review quotes it ("simply wrong", p. 5; "the rationality of survival, not of profit maximization", p. 105). Readers: Mann (1986, p. 574), "a new way of thinking about Chinese society". A contested contribution: Pomeranz rejects it (2000, p. 17; 2003), and the dispute is drawn separately.

edges.relationship: England and the Yangzi delta “at opposite poles” of development and involution by 1800: Pomeranz’s comparison criticised for resting on secondary evidence, omitting the English agricultural revolution and reversing coal supply and demand (2002; rejoinder 2003)
edges.evidence_note: Huang's review essay, JAS 61:2 (May 2002), 501–538 (Whole article OCRed; selected passages read closely, remaining text searched; map images not inspected): the book "is not built on original research, but rather relies on past secondary scholarship" (p. 502); "Pomeranz says nothing at all" about the English agricultural revolution (p. 502); on coal, "it is the lack of industrial demand that explains the non-development of China’s coal industry. Pomeranz’s argument, in short, places the cart before the horse" (p. 533); England and the delta "were in fact virtually at opposite poles in a continuum from development to involution", and the eighteenth-century delta held "the roots of a massive nineteenth-century social crisis" (p. 534). Rejoinder, JAS 62:1 (Feb. 2003), 157–167 (read in part): he concedes "a misplaced decimal" in his 1990 book (p. 157), says his case rests on "conditions of production", and reports that Pomeranz now grants declining average returns as cotton replaced grain (p. 158, quoting Pomeranz 2002, p. 547). Qualifications: Huang credits "a useful contribution" and the wish "to de-center Europe" (2002, p. 533). Pomeranz's answers are drawn on the reverse arrow. Restated in 2016 (Modern China 42:2, read in part by the second research pass): "Pomeranz's work makes this kind of basic factual error because it lacks any original research" (p. 136).

edges.relationship: Involution rejected: Chinese household labour read as an industrious-revolution pattern comparable to Europe’s (2000); in reply, involution called internally inconsistent and his evidence faulted for confusing marginal with average returns and for a misplaced decimal (2002–2003)
edges.evidence_note: Pomeranz's own words. The Great Divergence (2000, p. 17, re-read): Chinese families supposedly kept women and children working below a subsistence wage, "thus producing an 'involuted economy'; I will show that there is little reason to believe this" (n. 27: "P. Huang 1990: 11–17"); labour deployment instead resembles "Europe’s 'industrious revolution'". Reply, JAS 61:2 (2002), 539–590 (publisher extract only): "He also ignores plentiful new research on both Asia and Europe". Response, JAS 62:1 (Feb. 2003), 167–181 (read in part): Huang's "concept of 'involution' was internally inconsistent"; he "had repeatedly confused marginal and average returns", compared male, female and child labour indiscriminately, and made "a basic arithmetic mistake (a misplaced decimal)" (pp. 167–168); "a gathering consensus, pace Huang, about the timing of that divergence … invalidates various old explanations of it, including his" (p. 179). Qualification: per Huang (2003, p. 158), Pomeranz's 2002 reply grants that "A decline in average returns to labor as more people move from grain to cotton farming is still evident" (p. 547); the body of the reply is unread here.

edges.relationship: Unilinear modernization and “England-derived assumptions” questioned: commercialization need not end in capitalist development, and Chinese “paradoxes” expose assumptions shared by Western and Chinese models (1991, 2003)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, read. 1991 (p. 299): a "crisis of confidence in underlying, yet unspoken, assumptions that are shared by opposing constructs"; Chinese "feudalism" and "incipient capitalism" models and Western formalist ones share them (pp. 300–302); "We customarily assume that rural commercialization is powered by the profit-maximizing activities of enterprising farmers. That was the experience of Smith’s and Marx’s England" (p. 314); his aim was to show "how its dynamic and logic were different, producing results that appear paradoxical from our England-derived assumptions" (pp. 315–316). Rejoinder (2003, p. 164): "it was precisely the objection to unilineal modernizationism that originally drove my work and that of other social historians"; p. 165: "no single path or single causal factor to modern economic development". The critique is aimed at Smithian and Marxist assumptions alike; this arrow records its target in modernization theory, not a rejection of all comparison.

edges.relationship: Village-level social history of the North China peasantry from Japanese rural surveys, archives and interviews, an alternative to the gentry-society paradigm (1985)
edges.evidence_note: Readers' explicit claims, read. Mann (JAS, 1986): "This rich and ambitious work marks a new begining [sic] for social history in the China field" (p. 572); he combined Mantetsu survey data with Qing archives and interviews in "two of the same villages studied in the 1930s" (p. 572); his model is "an alternative to the gentry society paradigm that has dominated the field for decades" (p. 574). Duara (HJAS, 1986, p. 283): "a very adroit methodology which combines the use of intensive case studies with extensive quantitative data". Huang and Bernhardt (2024, p. 3) place Modern China's early symposia in "the rising wave of the 'new social history'". Qualifications: Duara doubts the evidence for excess labour (p. 286) and the solidary/atomized village typology (pp. 287–288).
edges.map_label: Village social history of North China, 1985

edges.relationship: Bourdieu’s “practice” and “logic of practice” taken into Chinese legal and rural history, recast as practice over historical time (1995–2005)
edges.evidence_note: His acknowledgement, read by the second research pass. 2005 (Modern China 31:2, n. 3): "Readers familiar with the writings of Pierre Bourdieu will recognize the source of the terms 'practice' and 'logic of practice' as they are used here"; Bourdieu "did not consider practice as process over time. My own preference, no doubt partly due to my bias as a historian, is for the study of practice as historical process." 1995 (Modern China 21:1, pp. 109–110): Bourdieu extended "Marxist structural analysis from the objective into the representational (or 'symbolic') realm" but "has not 'problematized' possible disjunctions between representational and objective realities". Civil Justice in China: Representation and Practice in the Qing (1996) carries the terms in its title; the book is unread. A modified borrowing, not adoption of Bourdieu’s whole theory.

edges.relationship: Against the “incipient capitalism” model: commercialization and wage labour in Ming–Qing China without capitalist development (1985–1998)
edges.evidence_note: His own texts. 1985 (p. 11, read by both passes): the Chinese "incipient capitalism" model, "First set forth by Mao (1939)", held that capitalism had "sprouted" before imperialism. 1991 (read in part by both passes): Chinese scholars "maintained that if Western imperialism had not intruded into China, the capitalist sprouts of the Ming and Qing would have led to transformative capitalist development" (p. 313, as the second pass reads it); "given China’s non-capitalist nineteenth century, what sense does it make to speak of the earlier period as incipient capitalist?" (p. 302). 1998 (p. 188, read by the second pass): "contrary to the predictions of Marxist theory, I simply could not find in 'managerial farming' substantial advances in productivity, despite its use of the 'capitalist production relations' of wage labor". A critique of a specific Marxist model, not of Marxian analysis as such: he credits Marxist and substantivist resources (Tilly, Paige; 1998, p. 186).

edges.relationship: Against “culturalism” in China studies: representations do not dissolve facts, and Orientalism’s later parts are “much less convincing” (1998)
edges.evidence_note: His own text, read by the second research pass ("Four Traps and a Question", Modern China 24:2, 1998, pp. 193–195): "While culturalist theories are surely correct to emphasize that facts come with constructed representations, I believe they are wrong to jump from there to the conclusion that facts are no more than representations … But that is the conclusion that is drawn by Said, on the theoretical inspiration of Michel Foucault" (he then quotes Orientalism, pp. 272–273); "Said's (1978) book, to be sure, makes effective and telling points, especially in the first part … But the discussions in the second and third parts are much less convincing. The connections drawn become more and more tenuous" (p. 195). A China historian's critique of Said, distinct from Said's own critique of Foucault (edge_971).

edges.relationship: Brenner and Isett challenge Pomeranz through social-property relations (2002); Broadberry and Gupta place the advanced parts of Asia with Europe’s stagnating periphery on wages and prices (2006); Allen and colleagues dispute Chinese–English urban real-wage parity (2011); Broadberry, Guan and Li place divergence between leading regions around 1700 (2021)
edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents four named interventions, not a verdict of the economic-history entry, which includes Pomeranz and his allies; each establishes something different. Brenner and Isett (JAS 61:2, 2002; online reprint read in part, no folios), on social-property relations: England's divergence came from "this already existing decisive divergence, not England’s capacity to gain access to the American colonies"; the delta followed "a Malthusian pattern", England "a Smithian pattern"; "Contra Pomeranz". Broadberry and Gupta (EHR 59:1, 2006; summary and pp. 2–3 read by the second research pass), on wages and prices: "Contrary to the claims of Pomeranz, Parthasarathi, and other 'world historians', the prosperous parts of Asia between 1500 and 1800 look similar to the stagnating southern, central, and eastern parts of Europe … The 'great divergence' … was already well underway before 1800" (p. 2). Allen, Bassino, Ma, Moll-Murata and van Zanden (EHR 2011, read pp. 8–9, 29–31), on urban real wages: "our findings also dispute the revisionists’ claim that the advanced parts of China, such as the Yangzi Delta, were on a par with England"; "Adam Smith’s pessimism looks closer to the truth than the revisionists’ optimism" (p. 31); they also find Chinese urban wages on a par with central and southern Europe, against the "rise of the west" literature (pp. 30–31). Broadberry, Guan and Li (JEH 2021, read pp. 958–959), on regional GDP per capita: "The Great Divergence thus began around 1700, earlier than originally suggested by the California School, but later than implied by earlier writers" (p. 958). The qualified chronology is theirs alone. None endorses Huang's involution, whose dispute with Pomeranz is drawn on its own arrows. Robert Brenner is not yet an atlas entry; if he becomes one, his critique with Isett moves to its own arrow.
edges.map_label: Property relations, wages and regional GDP, 2002–2021

edges.relationship: Historical scales and teaching after the nation: world history as comparison that tests “the universality or regional specificity of particular processes”, against curricula still organised by nation (AHA presidential address, 2014)
edges.evidence_note: His AHA presidential address, delivered 3 January 2014 and published in AHR 119:1 (2014), 1–22, read via WebFetch extraction of the AHA text (no pagination; the last fifth not covered). World history "makes comparisons that interrogate claims about the universality or regional specificity of particular processes"; he asks "how our discipline is responding and might respond to the changing geography of our own era"; in a survey of "218 AHA member departments", "46 percent of all classes" at the introductory level "were on national histories"; he warns that "most global history narratives thus far have been strongly materialistic, and focused on general processes"; and closes on "reframing for a less national age". A later programme statement, distinct from the 2000 method on edge_898.

edges.relationship: Consumer demand compared across Eurasian cores: sugar, cloth and “consumerist” attitudes in China, Japan and western Europe, with differences “small and of uncertain direction” (2000)
edges.evidence_note: His own summary of chapters 3–4 in the introduction (2000, pp. 17–18; read by both research passes): Part 2 "begins by moving away from survival-oriented activities to examine new kinds of consumer demand"; differences "in both quantities of goods available and 'consumerist' attitudes among these societies seem small and of uncertain direction. (For instance, mid-eighteenth-century Chinese almost certainly consumed more sugar than Europeans, and people in the Lower Yangzi core may have produced as much cloth per capita in 1750 as Britons did in 1800.)" The chapters themselves are unread. Contested by Huang (2002, p. 521, as the second pass reads it) and answered by Pomeranz (2003, p. 168: "probably the bottom 75 percent of the Jiangnan population lived at least as well as their English counterparts").

edges.relationship: Wallerstein’s world-system grouped with the “Europe-centered stories” whose motor is western Europe’s prior advantages; Pomeranz borrows from them but argues for a late, contingent divergence (2000)
edges.evidence_note: His own introduction (2000, pp. 14–16; read by both research passes). Braudel, Wallerstein and Chaudhuri appear with North in "a second group of arguments" that "emphasize the emergence of institutions in early modern Europe" (p. 14); "the motor of Wallerstein’s story is western Europe’s unique combination of relatively free labor, large and productive urban populations, and merchants and governments" (p. 15, as the second pass quotes it); "This work borrows from these arguments—mostly those of the various 'institutionalists'—but ultimately argues for different propositions" (p. 16). A bounded critique of a Eurocentric premise, not a rejection of unequal exchange: he cites Williams, Frank and Amin as earlier arguments from colonial extraction (p. 3 n. 2). The chapter discussions are unread.

edges.relationship: Revolutionary political culture: rhetoric, symbols and the social identity of a new political class (1984); the Revolution’s contradictory futures of terror, democracy and human rights (AHA address, 2003)
edges.evidence_note: Existing reading of Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (hunt_political_culture: primary chapter openings at pp. 87, 123, 149 and 213; the contents keep both a "poetics of power" and a sociology of politics with quantitative appendices). Her AHA presidential address (AHR 108:1, 2003; read via WebFetch extraction, no pagination) asks "how could the French Revolution produce such contradictory consequences?", holds that it "also gave birth to human rights and democracy", and defines cultural revolution as "the politicization of everyday life" (n. 42, as the second research pass locates it). Her contribution to political history; edge_355 records the same 1984 book's contribution to cultural history.

edges.relationship: Practical realism with Joyce Appleby and Margaret Jacob (1994) and a reassessment of the cultural turn with Victoria Bonnell (1999)
edges.evidence_note: Existing readings. Telling the Truth about History (appleby_hunt_jacob): all three authors share every chapter; the chapter 7 "Practical Realism" section and notes name Putnam and Peirce as resources; chapter 8: "It is time to come out of the trenches." Beyond the Cultural Turn (bonnell_hunt_primary): the editors' introduction (pp. 1, 12–25 read) presents competing reassessments and explicitly acknowledges White's disagreement in his afterword. A particular response within the debate, not its resolution; co-author credits retained.
edges.map_label: Practical realism and beyond the cultural turn, 1994–99

edges.relationship: Globalization as the paradigm succeeding Marxism, modernization, Annales and identity politics, questioned for privileging economics and for threatening the gains of cultural history, as her reviewer summarises Writing History in the Global Era (2014)
edges.evidence_note: Reviewer evidence only; the book is unread here. Julia McClure (Reviews in History 1732, 2015; read via WebFetch extraction, and in full by the second research pass) summarises the argument: globalization has become a dominant "paradigm" replacing Marxism, modernization, the Annales school and identity politics; it privileges economics and macro trends and risks overshadowing "society" and "self"; and it "potentially threatens to wash away the gains of the last decades of cultural history" (Hunt, p. 59, as McClure quotes her). McClure criticises Hunt for not naming proponents of the paradigm and for treating world or global history as the history of globalization. This atlas was first developed around the book; its own words should replace this reviewer summary when read. Further pages as McClure quotes them: globalization "asserts the inescapability of the process, the primacy of economics in driving it" (p. 55); "historians need to contest the terrain it now claims, using the tools held out by cultural theories" (p. 43). McClure: her criticism "is not a criticism of historical genre, but of ideology".
edges.map_label: Writing History in the Global Era, 2014 (per McClure)

edges.relationship: Human rights made “self-evident” through imagined empathy, epistolary novels and the rejection of torture, 1760s–1790s, as reviewers summarise Inventing Human Rights (2007)
edges.evidence_note: Reviewer evidence only; the book is unread here. David A. Bell (LRB, 15 November 2007; read via WebFetch extraction) summarises it: epistolary novels such as Pamela, Clarissa and Julie taught readers to identify with others; torture was condemned by the 1780s; a "logic of rights" followed the 1789 Declaration; he calls the method "the new cultural history", which Hunt had popularised, and finds the 2007 book keeping the thesis of The Family Romance of the French Revolution (1992). Samuel Moyn (The Nation, 16 April 2007) reports her dating of the cause to "the Enlightenment and the age of democratic revolutions" and "the cascading logic of human rights". Their criticisms are drawn on the critique arrow from intellectual history. A second contribution to cultural history, distinct from the 1989 introduction (edge_756).

edges.relationship: Inventing Human Rights criticised for reading late-twentieth-century human rights back into the eighteenth century and for making “rights themselves” its protagonists (Moyn, 2007), and for a cultural-history method that flattens texts and actions (Bell, 2007)
edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Samuel Moyn's and David A. Bell's specified criticisms, not a verdict of intellectual history. Moyn (The Nation, 16 April 2007; complete text read via WebFetch extraction): the new human-rights history "distorts the past to suit the present"; "rights talk" had "historical lineages completely different from humanitarianism"; "The protagonists of her book are not people thinking and acting on their convictions but rights themselves"; there is "little reason to locate the 'invention' of human rights as we now know them in the late eighteenth century", since they are "an invention of recent date". Bell (LRB 29:22, 15 November 2007; complete text read via WebFetch extraction): the account after 1789 through the present is compressed into 38 pages, concentrating on 1948, novels crowd out theatre and painting, ordinary people who read no novels also embraced rights, and the new cultural history tends to flatten the difference between texts and actions; he still calls the book "a rich, elegant and persuasive essay". Moyn's later book-length argument (The Last Utopia, 2010) is unread here.
edges.map_label: Moyn and Bell on Inventing Human Rights, 2007

edges.relationship: Moral economies of science: certain forms of empiricism, quantification and objectivity “require” a web of affect-saturated values (1995)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read (Osiris 10, 1995, pp. 3–4). "certain forms of empiricism, quantification, and objectivity itself are not simply compatible with moral economies; they require moral economies" (p. 3); a moral economy is "a web of affect-saturated values that stand and function in well-defined relationship to one another" (p. 4). n. 2 gathers studies by Hannaway, Porter, Schaffer and Shapin under the rubric. A distinct contribution from the 1992 image article (edge_761); the later book Objectivity (2007, with Galison) is dated in the chronology and read only through a reviewer.

edges.relationship: Science studies and the history of science diverged during the 1990s: the history of science “became ever more historical and science studies ever less”; science studies stayed “undisciplined”, and historicizing objectivity is not debunking it (2009)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read in full (Critical Inquiry 35, 2009). The fields "came to diverge … as the history of science became ever more historical and science studies ever less" (p. 800); science studies read Kuhn "as a manifesto of relativism", historians took from him that "teleology must be repudiated" (p. 802); the history of science "has … become a discipline", while science studies "has remained interdisciplinary—and, even on the testimony of some insiders, undisciplined" (p. 811); its assumptions are "Manichean" (p. 812). In the terms of the Science Wars she answers the relativism charge: "to historicize the category of the fact, objectivity, or proof is not thereby to debunk it" (p. 812); "'If historical, then relative' is a non sequitur" (p. 813), citing Latour's "Why Has Critique Run out of Steam?" (2004). Qualifications: she credits "intensive and fruitful exchanges" in the 1970s and 1980s (p. 800), doubts that disciplinarity is an unmixed good (p. 811 n. 30) and calls for "a new form of interdisciplinarity" (p. 813).
edges.map_label: Daston: history of science versus science studies, 2009

edges.relationship: Foucault’s historicism and the history of objectivity: Daston credits it with opening “proof, experience, and objectivity” to history (2009), and reviewers compare Objectivity with Foucauldian genealogy while noting its distance from his “epistemes”
edges.evidence_note: A comparison, not a documented personal borrowing. Her field-level acknowledgement, read (Critical Inquiry, 2009): the counterweight to miniaturizing history of science "has been supplied not by science studies but by a still more thoroughgoing form of historicism, namely, the philosophical history of Michel Foucault" (p. 809); "Topics like proof, experience, and objectivity … suddenly seemed fair game" (p. 810). Readers: Switzer (Foucault Studies 6, 2009, p. 99, read): "though it is unacknowledged, it is by a kind of Foucauldian genealogy that Daston and Galison conduct their study"; Henning (New Formations 64, 2008, read in full by the second research pass): virtues are aimed at through "'techniques of the self' in Foucault's sense, though this is not a straightforwardly Foucaultian argument" (p. 154), and the authors "distance themselves from Foucault's theory of historical rupture" (p. 157). Objectivity itself contrasts its history with "the static tableaux of paradigms and epistemes" (p. 19, as Switzer quotes it); the book is unread here and Galison holds equal credit. Personal transmission can be reconsidered after stronger evidence is read.

edges.relationship: Two explicitly distinguished uses of “moral economy”: the crowd’s “legitimizing notion” (1971) and the affect-laden values of science (1995)
edges.evidence_note: Daston's own note, read (Osiris 10, 1995, p. 3 n. 1): "my use of the term moral economy diverges significantly from E. P. Thompson's in 'The Moral Economy of the English Crowd in the Eighteenth Century' … My appeal here to 'economies' of affects and values has little to do with Thompson's accounts of corn markets and the tradition of 'setting the price' by persuasion or riot, although it does appeal to a broader sense of 'legitimizing notion.'" A teaching comparison of one term in two fields, not an influence: she says the usage diverges. Thompson's essay is recorded on edge_472.

edges.relationship: Elias’s civilizing process as a model for the collective self-discipline of scientific observers (1995)
edges.evidence_note: Her acknowledgement, read by the second research pass ("The Moral Economy of Science", Osiris 10, 1995, pp. 3–5 and 21–24, in the IAS-hosted scan). n. 7: "I have in mind a gradual shaping of a collective personality akin (and, as will be seen below, sometimes identical) to Norbert Elias's 'civilizing process'"; p. 22: "Norbert Elias argued that all complex coordinations of human activity partake of the 'civilizing process,' that is, the 'permanent self-control' demanded by 'the lengthening of the chains of social action and interdependence,' and science is no exception here." She applies it to the self-effacement of "aperspectival objectivity" (pp. 21–22). Compare elias → roger_chartier (edge_453).

edges.relationship: Williams’s Capitalism and Slavery tested on the compensation records: supported on slave-wealth in British society, qualified on decline, and set against a British Marxist pantheon that left James and Williams out (2009–2014)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read (History Workshop Journal 78, 2014). "C. L. R James and Eric Williams did not appear in their pantheon. James and Williams, in their struggle against racism and colonialism insisted on the linkage between metropole and colony … the intimate connections … between capitalism and slavery" (p. 23). "Williams never argued that slavery 'caused' the Industrial Revolution … as Nicholas Draper, Keith McClelland and I suggest in the co-authored book which documents the results of the first phase of our project on the Legacies of British Slave-Ownership (LBS), there is a move to a modified version of Williams’s thesis amongst economic historians" (p. 24); "Williams’s insight into the importance of slave-derived wealth to eighteenth-century society and culture has been greatly expanded" (p. 24). Qualifications: the modified thesis is attributed jointly to the LBS authors and set among economic historians (Pomeranz, Inikori); it is not a claim that slavery caused industrialization. The jointly written introduction to Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014; read in part by the second research pass, without print pages) tests Williams directly: "Eric Williams' Capitalism and Slavery included four connected arguments that are critical for us"; "our findings are entirely supportive of Williams in the context of this second thesis" (slave-wealth in British society); on industrialisation "Our material cannot resolve these controversies"; and the work "complicates Williams by qualifying his 'decline' thesis". Katie Donington, a co-author, recalls that "The project foregrounded Williams's work" (Black Perspectives, 2020). Hall was the project's principal investigator (REF 2014 case study).

edges.relationship: Class as the key dynamic questioned: Hobsbawm and his fellow Marxist historians, aware of plantation economies, left “race, slavery and the Caribbean” outside their concern; gender and race proposed as analytics of capital formation (2014)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read (History Workshop Journal 78, 2014, a lecture at the conference "History after Hobsbawm"). He "was critical of the cultural turn"; "Feminist history, in his view, was at best interested in 'winning collective recognition'"; postcolonial approaches "were not on his radar beyond the work of Subaltern Studies" (p. 22). "Hobsbawm was well aware of the significance of plantation economies to the development of industrial capitalism" (p. 23), but "his concern, and that of his fellow Marxist historians, was not with race, slavery and the Caribbean" (p. 23); "While class was the key historical dynamic in his analytic work, gender and race have become key analytics for our 'interesting times'" (p. 24). Qualifications: a critique within a shared agenda, "connecting these insights with older Marxist traditions" (p. 22); she credits Industry and Empire on colonial markets (p. 23). Distinct from the critiques by Chakrabarty (edge_917) and Guha (edge_979).
edges.map_label: Hall: after Hobsbawm, gender and race, 2014

edges.relationship: Metropole and colony made together: Birmingham abolitionists, Baptist missionaries and Jamaica, and the shift from paternalist hopes to racial thinking, 1830–1867 (2002)
edges.evidence_note: Her own statement of the book's argument, read by the second research pass ("A Response to the Commentators", JBS 42:4, 2003): "The central argument of Civilising Subjects is that being a colonizer was part of the construction of Englishness in the nineteenth century" (p. 530); splitting the narrative between Jamaica and Birmingham meant "reasserting the gap between metropole and colony as fundamental to the maintenance of metropolitan power" (p. 534). A reader's explicit claim and her own description, read; the book is unread here. Woollacott (Connected Worlds, 2006, chapter 4, read in part): "The great strengths, in postcolonial terms, of Hall’s magnum opus include … her compelling insistence on the interconstitutive connections between colony and metropole; her interest in the historical construction of race and its connections to gender and class; and perhaps above all, her political engagement with the operation of imperialism and colonialism and their legacies." Hall (History Workshop Journal, 2014, p. 22): "As a protagonist of feminist and postcolonial work". The University of Chicago Press description: "the idea of empire was at the heart of mid-nineteenth-century British self-imagining"; by the 1860s "a harsher racial vocabulary". Woollacott notes its limit: no connections "between Jamaica and other colonies beyond Edward John Eyre’s career".

edges.relationship: Civilising Subjects praised for showing that “empire is always on top of what it rules”, but faulted for not drawing on Subaltern Studies for unrecorded colonised voices and for treating culture as propaganda rather than analysing how it disguised colonial violence (2003)
edges.evidence_note: Said's review, "Always on Top" (LRB 25:6, 20 March 2003; complete text read via WebFetch extraction, no pagination). Praise: "Hall’s excellent book"; a "dialectical" history linking ideas, institutions and daily life; it shows that "empire is always on top of what it rules". Criticisms: sermons, polemics, letters and philosophy are treated alike as "evidence"; she does not draw on Ranajit Guha and the Subaltern Studies group (Woollacott 2006 quotes him: Hall "mystifyingly doesn’t draw" on them); her treatment of culture as propaganda follows John MacKenzie and neglects how culture, in Arnold, Carlyle and Dickens, insulated and disguised colonial violence. A mixed review whose criticisms are specific and methodological; he frames the book with Culture and Imperialism's "intertwined histories".

edges.relationship: Legacies of British Slave-ownership: slave-owners compensated at emancipation traced into British commerce, politics and culture, with gender and race as forces in capital formation (project from 2009; book and essay 2014; with Draper, McClelland and colleagues)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read (History Workshop Journal 78, 2014): "Since 2009 a team of historians at University College London, of whom I am one, have been investigating slave-owners" (p. 24); from "Nick Draper’s study of the compensation records" they "documented all the claimants to compensation at the time of emancipation – when twenty million pounds was paid to the slave-owners" (p. 26); slave-ownership is "a way of bringing slavery home and problematizing whiteness" (p. 25); the essay "argues that gender and race are both critical to capital formation … Classical Marxist accounts of the development of industrial capitalism need to be rethought" (abstract). The 2014 book, co-authored with Draper, McClelland, Donington and Lang, is read through its publisher abstract: "one powerful way in which Empire came home to Victorian Britain". Burnard (JWH, opening) calls it "this outstanding collection of essays". Collective work; all credits retained.

edges.relationship: The Black Jacobins as a model for analysing “metropole and colony in one lens” (2003)
edges.evidence_note: Her own acknowledgement, read by the second research pass (JBS 42:4, 2003, p. 533): "Colonizers were made both in the metropole and on colonial sites. And, as C. L. R. James's The Black Jacobins (1938) taught us, much can be gained through the analysis of metropole and colony in one lens." A retrospective acknowledgement made in defending the book's method; it names a resource, not the origin of her project. Her 2014 essay also sets James and Williams against the British Marxist pantheon (History Workshop Journal 78, p. 23, read).
edges.map_label: Metropole and colony in one lens, 2003

edges.relationship: Fanon’s claim that colonialism shaped the colonizers as much as the colonized frames the question of how empire was lived “at home” (2002–2003)
edges.evidence_note: Her own statement, read by the second research pass (JBS 42:4, 2003, p. 530): "Yet if, as Frantz Fanon argued, colonialism shaped the colonizers as much as the colonized then how was this expressed in everyday culture? How was it lived 'at home' as well as in the empire?" One explicit sentence framing the project; the Fanon text is not specified. Not to be confused with edge_418 (fanon → identity), which concerns Stuart Hall.

edges.relationship: Slave-ownership reinscribed into modern British history: the Legacies of British Slave-ownership project and its database of about 46,000 compensation claims (2009–2014; with Draper, McClelland and colleagues)
edges.evidence_note: Read by the second research pass. REF 2014 case study (WebFetch excerpts): the ESRC project ran 1 June 2009 to 31 May 2012, led by "Professor Hall and her research associates, Dr Nicholas Draper and Dr Keith McClelland", and from "the records of the £20m paid in compensation to slave-owners in 1833" documented "the c.46,000 individual claims and awards". 2014 introduction (excerpts, no print pages): "our project is to reinscribe slave-ownership onto modern British history"; "The database digitises all the awards in the slave-compensation records of the 1830s". Hall (History Workshop Journal, 2014, p. 25, read): "a way of bringing slavery home". Lucky Valley (2024; publisher abstract) extends the work to Edward Long and "racial capitalism". Collective work; all credits retained. Distinct from the economic-history arrow, which records her argument about capital formation.

edges.relationship: A public Encyclopaedia of British Slave-ownership, accompanied by workshops with local and family historians and correspondence with descendants of slave-owners and the enslaved (2010–2013).
edges.evidence_note: Read by the second research pass. REF 2014 case study (WebFetch excerpts): workshops drew "mostly local and family historians from outside academia"; correspondents were "the great majority from descendants of slave-owners and the enslaved"; the online Encyclopaedia of British Slave-ownership launched on 28 February 2013 and had 137,998 visits from 108,022 unique visitors to 31 July 2013. The 2014 introduction names responsibilities "to the descendants of the enslaved people, to the descendants of the slave-owners and to other academic and non-academic constituencies" and says the project "has no position on reparations and restitution". An institutional impact statement and the team's own account; collective work. The atlas owner's separate Early Atlantic World project uses LBS-derived data; nothing from it is evidence here.

edges.relationship: Englishness as a formation of class, gender and race: imperial men, masculinities and “raced” white subjects (2002–2003)
edges.evidence_note: Her own retrospective statement, read by the second research pass (JBS 42:4, 2003): her task was "to analyze the 'racing,' to use Toni Morrison's term, of white subjects, the ways in which Englishness needs to be understood not only as a formation of class and of gender, but also of race and ethnicity" (p. 531); the book "is about men, masculinities, and the making of 'raced' subjects" (p. 536); she concedes to Holt and Levine that "There is undoubtedly more that I could have done with the women" (pp. 536–537). Civilising Subjects itself is unread. Distinct from the 1987 Family Fortunes contribution, which reaches gender history through edge_757's social-history claim and the existing roster row.

edges.relationship: The national “island story” rethought through empire: the history taught in schools and universities “needed to be rethought through the frame of empire” (2003)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read by the second research pass (JBS 42:4, 2003): race politics in postcolonial Britain "posed a challenge to the national story, the 'island story' of the homogeneity of the English-British nation" (p. 530); "One of my self-appointed tasks was to demonstrate the ways in which the well-established narrative of British history, the national history, the one taught in schools and universities, needed to be rethought through the frame of empire. Civilising Subjects is not only cultural and social history, it is also political history" (p. 537). Macaulay and Son (2012) extends the critique to Macaulay's History of England, as Tao Wei (Essays in History, 2014, read in full by the second pass) reads it: Hall calls him "one of the most influential proponents of liberal imperial discourse" (p. xiii); that book is unread and the edge rests on the 2003 statement.

verification.note: Complete text read via WebFetch extraction for revision 1.144 (no pagination). Bell's summary: epistolary novels (Pamela, Clarissa, Julie) taught identification with others; torture condemned by the 1780s; a "logic of rights" after 1789. Criticisms: the account after 1789 through the present is compressed into 38 pages, concentrating on 1948 (the second research pass quotes "the period after 1789 'in a breezy 38 pages'"); he reports Moyn's criticism and calls it "partly misplaced"; novels at the expense of theatre, painting and emulation; causation hinted at; ordinary people who did not read novels also embraced rights; the "new cultural history" tends to flatten texts and actions. He calls her French Revolution studies "luminous", reads The Family Romance (1992) as tracing family imagery from paternal monarchy to fraternal republic, a thesis the 2007 book keeps, and credits her with popularising "the new cultural history". Verdict: "a rich, elegant and persuasive essay" that "raises more questions than it can answer".

edge_899.evidence_note: Pomeranz's own argument, The Great Divergence (2000), introduction (pp. 3–27 read; later-edition pagination). He takes 'Why wasn’t England the Yangzi Delta?' as seriously as 'Why wasn’t the Yangzi Delta England?' and argues 'that Europe, too, could have wound up on an “east Asian,” labor-intensive path', a result avoided through 'sharp discontinuities, based on both fossil fuels and access to New World resources' (p. 13). 'Constraints connected to energy, and ultimately to quantities of land (particularly the shrinking forests of core areas throughout Eurasia), were a far more important looming impediment to further growth' than capital (p. 19). The Atlantic trade mattered for 'how much they relieved the strain on Europe’s supply of what was truly scarce: land and energy', and 'the fruits of overseas exploitation were probably roughly as important to at least Britain’s economic transformation as its epochal turn to fossil fuels' (p. 23). The book uses 'the fruits of overseas coercion' to explain the difference from China and Japan, 'not the whole of that development' (p. 4). Cooper's 2000 review (read in full) summarises it in the same year: 'Europe had more institutional slack, easier access to coal (which was crucial, in the author's view), and cheap imports of sugar and cotton harvested by slaves in its New World colonies', and objects that Pomeranz 'relies heavily on plausible guesstimates'. The earlier Making of a Hinterland (1993) already argued, in the publisher's description, 'that the development of certain regions entailed the systematic underdevelopment of other regions'; Bianco (1996, p. 243, read) notes that it 'ne sépare jamais l'enquête régionale du débat théorique', including Huang's involution model. A contribution, not a founding: earlier arguments from colonial extraction (Williams 1944, Frank 1969, Amin 1974) are cited at p. 3, n. 2, and he notes parallels with Sugihara (p. 12). Huang's 2002 critique and Pomeranz's reply are later readings, not evidence for this edge. Revision 1.144: the critiques now have their own arrows (philip_huang → kenneth_pomeranz; economic → kenneth_pomeranz). Pomeranz restated the timing in 2003: "a gathering consensus, pace Huang, about the timing of that divergence" (JAS 62:1, p. 179, read). Catherine Hall reads the coal-and-colonies argument as part of "a modified version of Williams’s thesis amongst economic historians": "Pomeranz sees the Atlantic slave-economy and the availability of coal as the two complementary factors allowing Britain to expand" (History Workshop Journal 78, 2014, p. 24, read).

edge_898.evidence_note: Pomeranz's own statement of method, The Great Divergence (2000), introduction (pp. 3–27 read; later-edition pagination). Comparisons between scattered core regions should be 'truly reciprocal' (p. 8), 'viewing both sides of the comparison as “deviations” when seen through the expectations of the other, rather than leaving one as always the norm' (p. 8). With Tilly's 'encompassing comparison', 'comparison and the analysis of connections become indistinguishable' (p. 10). 'Thus the book combines comparative analysis, some purely local contingency, and an integrative or global approach', and before 1800 'we have, instead, a polycentric world with no dominant center' (p. 4). The introduction ends 'with connections and interactions explaining what comparison alone cannot' (p. 25). He places the book as 'joining the burgeoning field of “world history,”' while warning that it 'treats the world’s regions very unevenly' and that 'adding a few Chinese and Japanese foils to a European story does not make it “world history”' (p. 25). A contribution, not a founding: the approach was 'anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong' (p. 7), and 'Here, too, I am following a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed' (p. 8); the encompassing comparison is Tilly's (p. 10, n. 14). Huang's 2002 critique and Pomeranz's reply are later readings, not evidence for this edge. Revision 1.144: later reception of the method. Pomeranz was a co-founding editor of the Journal of Global History, which began publication in 2006 (AHA biography, as the second research pass reads it). Its editors wrote in 2021 that the Great Divergence debate "was a major inspiration for the foundation of the Journal in 2006" and that "comparisons and connections" had been "elaborated perhaps most fruitfully in the context of large-scale reciprocal comparisons" (Frankema, Sood and Tworek, JGH 16:1, pp. 1–2, read in full by the second pass); they do not name Pomeranz.

text_revisions.new: A historian of China whose reciprocal comparisons of Eurasian core regions recast the divergence of European and Chinese economies. The Great Divergence (2000) takes 'Why wasn’t England the Yangzi Delta?' as seriously as the reverse question and argues that 'Europe, too, could have wound up on an “east Asian,” labor-intensive path'. Coal, and land-intensive goods from New World colonies worked by enslaved people, relieved Europe's constraints of land and energy. The earlier Making of a Hinterland (1993), in its publisher’s description and Bianco’s review, traces the economic and ecological costs for inland North China when the late Qing and Republican state abandoned many hinterland areas. The Great Divergence became central to the debate over the “California School”. Philip Huang answered that England and the Yangzi delta stood “at opposite poles” of development and involution (2002–2003); Brenner and Isett located England’s divergence in early modern social-property relations (2002); Broadberry and Gupta found the advanced parts of Asia closer to Europe’s stagnating periphery in wages and prices (2006); Allen and colleagues disputed urban real-wage parity between the Yangzi delta and England (2011); and Broadberry, Guan and Li placed the divergence between leading regions around 1700 (2021). He was a co-founding editor of the Journal of Global History (2006), and his AHA presidential address (2014) asked how history might be reframed “for a less national age”.

Bin Wong', takes the 'encompassing comparison' from Charles Tilly, and notes parallels with Sugihara Kaoru. Arguments from colonial extraction (Williams, Frank, Amin) precede his. text_revisions.new: This entry presents the argument of The Great Divergence as its introduction states it (pp. 3–27 read, with the contents, in a preview of the later Princeton edition; page numbers are that edition's). The Making of a Hinterland is checked at contents level and through Bianco's 1996 review, read in full; its text is unread. He is not presented as the originator of reciprocal comparison: he writes that the approach was 'anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong', takes the 'encompassing comparison' from Charles Tilly, and notes parallels with Sugihara Kaoru. Arguments from colonial extraction (Williams, Frank, Amin) precede his. His estimates are contested: Cooper (2000) notes 'plausible guesstimates', and Bianco (1996) judges that the 1993 book 'postule plus qu'il ne prouve' a deliberate strategy of selective development. Later critiques (Huang 2002–2003; Brenner and Isett 2002; Broadberry and Gupta 2006; Allen and colleagues 2011; Broadberry, Guan and Li 2021) appear as critique arrows and do not change what the 2000 introduction is read as arguing. The ‘California School’ is a label for Pomeranz, Wong and colleagues (AHA biography), not an atlas entry. The 2014 address is read through the AHA web text without pagination; the 2009 essay is dated from its opening only.

text_revisions.old: Reassesses the explanatory models of social history in her introduction to The New Cultural History. She recognizes turns toward culture within Marxist and Annales histories while questioning the priority assigned to social experience.
text_revisions.new: A historian of the French Revolution whose Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (1984) joined revolutionary symbols and rhetoric to the sociology of political actors, using Geertz’s interpretive frame, and whose introduction to The New Cultural History (1989) reassessed the explanatory models of social history, recognising turns toward culture within Marxist and Annales histories while questioning the priority assigned to social experience. With Joyce Appleby and Margaret Jacob she defended a “practical realism” (1994), and with Victoria Bonnell she edited Beyond the Cultural Turn (1999). In her AHA presidential address (2003) she asked how the Revolution could “produce such contradictory consequences” as terror, democracy and human rights. Inventing Human Rights (2007), which reviewers summarise as tracing rights to imagined empathy, novels and the rejection of torture, was contested by Samuel Moyn and David A. Bell. Writing History in the Global Era (2014), the book around which this atlas was first developed, argued, in her reviewer’s summary, that globalization had become a new paradigm that could wash away the gains of cultural history.

Her political-culture work rests on the existing reading of the 1984 book’s chapter openings, and her later revolution argument on the 2003 address read through the AHA web text. text_revisions.old: With Peter Galison, investigates changing scientific ideals of objectivity through images and atlas-making. Their 1992 article distinguishes mechanical objectivity from other historically formed components of the concept.
text_revisions.new: A historian of science who historicizes the categories of scientific knowing. Her books include Classical Probability in the Enlightenment (1988) and, with Katharine Park, Wonders and the Order of Nature, 1150–1750 (1998). In “The Moral Economy of Science” (1995) she argued that certain forms of empiricism, quantification and objectivity “require moral economies”, “a web of affect-saturated values”, drawing on Elias’s civilizing process and distinguishing her sense of the term from E. P. Thompson’s. With Peter Galison she studied objectivity itself: their 1992 article distinguishes mechanical objectivity from other historically formed components of the concept, and their book Objectivity (2007) treats it, in reviewers’ readings, as one epistemic virtue beside others rather than their successor. She was a director at the Max Planck Institute for the History of Science from 1995 until 2019. In 2009 she argued that the history of science had become “a discipline” while science studies remained “undisciplined”, and that “to historicize the category of the fact, objectivity, or proof is not thereby to debunk it”.

text_revisions.old: Adds a substantive history-of-science contribution beyond gender history. Galison retains equal authorship and argument credit. Their historical analysis does not assert that scientific objectivity is simply impossible.
text_revisions.new: Adds a substantive history-of-science contribution beyond gender history. Galison retains equal authorship and argument credit for the 1992 article and the 2007 book, and Park for Wonders. Their historical analysis does not assert that scientific objectivity is simply impossible: in 2009 she wrote that “‘If historical, then relative’ is a non sequitur”. The 1995 and 2009 essays are read in her own words; Objectivity and Rules remain unread: their content is mediated by reviewers (Switzer and Henning; Lahav) and Rules by its publisher’s description, and the 1988 and 1998 books are dated from her 2009 author note and the Collège de France biography and carry no argument here. “Historical epistemology” in her sense is not the French tradition of the atlas’s Historical epistemology entry, and no edge connects them.

text_revisions.old: With Leonore Davidoff, relates English middle-class formation to gender, family, religion and economic life in Family Fortunes. Class identities and gender relations are investigated together rather than in separate historical accounts.
text_revisions.new: A historian of gender, class, race and empire. With Leonore Davidoff she related English middle-class formation to gender, family, religion and economic life in Family Fortunes (1987), investigating class identities and gender relations together rather than in separate accounts. Civilising Subjects (2002), whose “central argument”, she wrote, “is that being a colonizer was part of the construction of Englishness”, followed Birmingham abolitionists and Baptist missionaries to Jamaica; she credited C. L. R. James with showing what can be gained by studying “metropole and colony in one lens”. Angela Woollacott (2006) reads it as postcolonial history for its “insistence on the interconstitutive connections between colony and metropole”, and Edward Said (2003) praised it while asking for subaltern voices. From 2009 she led, with her research associates Nicholas Draper and Keith McClelland, University College London’s Legacies of British Slave-ownership project, tracing the slave-owners compensated at emancipation into Victorian Britain. In 2014 she and her coauthors identified a move toward modified versions of Williams’s thesis among economic historians, and she argued, against the British Marxist historians’ neglect of “race, slavery and the Caribbean”, that gender and race shaped the formation of capital. Lucky Valley (2024) turns to Edward Long and “racial capitalism”.

text_revisions.old: Family Fortunes: Men and Women of the English Middle Class 1780–1850 (1987). Joint work; retain all coauthor credits.
text_revisions.new: With Leonore Davidoff, Family Fortunes: Men and Women of the English Middle Class 1780–1850 (1987); White, Male and Middle Class (1992); with Keith McClelland and Jane Rendall, Defining the Victorian Nation (2000); Civilising Subjects: Metropole and Colony in the English Imagination, 1830–1867 (2002); Macaulay and Son: Architects of Imperial Britain (2012); with Nicholas Draper, Keith McClelland, Katie Donington and Rachel Lang, Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014); “Gendering Property, Racing Capital” (History Workshop Journal, 2014); Lucky Valley: Edward Long and the History of Racial Capitalism (2024). Joint works; retain all coauthor credits. Readings: Said (2003); Gikandi, Levine and Holt (JBS, 2003, as Hall answers them); Woollacott (2006); Tao Wei (2014).

text_revisions.new: Equal coauthor credit with Davidoff for Family Fortunes, whose newly checked evidence is the indexed prologue abstract and publisher description of a later edition. Family Fortunes and her imperial and slavery work (2002–2014) are distinct projects linked by attention to gender, class and race. The Legacies of British Slave-ownership is collective work and its edges credit the team. Her 2014 History Workshop Journal essay is read in her own words; Civilising Subjects is presented through her own 2003 reply to its commentators (pp. 530–537, read by a second research pass), Said’s and Woollacott’s readings and its publisher description; the commentators’ own texts are unread; Legacies is read through its jointly written introduction in excerpts without print pages and UCL’s 2014 impact case study; Macaulay and Son through Tao Wei’s review; White, Male and Middle Class, Defining the Victorian Nation and Lucky Valley through contents or publisher descriptions only. She is not Stuart Hall.
